title: Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan

epigraph.quote: Confronted with a like challenge to distill the secret of sound investment into three words, we venture the motto, Margin of Safety.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor

web_blocks.text: The verdict for new money is WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, conviction tier TIER_3, strategy bucket TACTICAL_MOMENTUM. Greaves closed at ₹225.97 on 13 November 2026 [108]. We would buy only inside ₹205.02–211.26, around the 10-week exponential moving average (EMA, a price average that weights recent weeks more) of ₹208.14, and we would drop the idea on a daily close below ₹197.60. The facts ledger still carries the 12 November bar at ₹223.18; the TradingView snapshot, taken after the 13 November close, is one bar newer and every level in this chapter uses it [108]. The Zerodha account does not hold Greaves, so there is nothing to sell. The chapter argues each side at full strength, turns the argument into a probability-weighted value, and names the price or event that would change the call.

web_blocks.caption: Bull and bear steelman, line by line, from the Pass 1 evidence
rows: Core earnings
The standalone engine business held a 13–14% EBITDA margin for three years, and core revenue grew 20% in H1 FY27 [1][6].
Core EBITDA margin fell from 14.9% to 12.0% in H1 FY27 on 20% more revenue, and management admits recovery is slower than planned [1][24].
Demand
Medium-horsepower gensets grew 35%, auto engines 37% and Excel 30% in the latest quarter, with the genset market growing 10–12% a year [1][62][27].
Growth is arriving before margin, and the diesel three-wheeler engine pool that funds the profit is shrinking [1][70].
GEML unit economics
The loss per scooter shrank from about ₹20,000 to ₹6,300, and revenue doubled in H1 FY27 [62][1].
GEML lost ₹63 crore at EBITDA in H1 FY27, and breakeven is promised “fairly soon” with no date [1][24].
Funding and cash
A ₹530 crore rights issue covers GEML’s burn for 12–18 months, and the core holds ₹110 crore of net cash [2][62].
Group operating cash flow was −₹212 crore in H1 FY27, and borrowings reached ₹513 crore at September 2026 [2][118].
Policy and history
The subsidy is now capped at ₹5,000 a vehicle, and the receivable is under ₹13 crore [75].
FAME-II cost about ₹477 crore and cut FY24 volume 56%, so subsidy rules can bite again [8][36].
Management and ambition
Four senior leaders are new, bad news is disclosed plainly, and the stated plan is 16–20% organic growth [24][28].
Three promises were met, five partly and two missed, and the ₹15,000 crore FY30 vision needs growth we rate under one-in-ten [28][6].
web_blocks.takeaway: The two columns agree on the facts and disagree on which fact sets the price. The bull values the engine business and treats GEML as a funded option; the bear values the cash the group actually produced and treats GEML as a recurring call on parent capital [1][2].

web_blocks.text: Each side is strongest on a different clock. The bull is stronger over 24 months on the core, because raw-material pass-through has a dated path, with OEM contract relief starting in Q4 FY27 [62]. The bear is stronger on the group’s cash, because the turn in operating cash flow has no date in any filing [2][24]. We therefore weight the cases 25% bull, 45% base and 30% bear. The bear is slightly more likely than the bull. The bear case loses 32.7% while the base case gains 34.1%, and the 5-point tilt toward the bear lowers the weighted value from about ₹302 to ₹288.7 (our calculation [118]).

web_blocks.the_number: Probability-weighted value of ₹288.7 a share in 24 months (November 2028), +27.8% against the ₹225.97 close, about 13.0% a year, and +38.7% against the ₹208.14 support level, about 17.8% a year.
web_blocks.how_calculated: 0.25 × ₹427 + 0.45 × ₹303 + 0.30 × ₹152 = ₹106.75 + ₹136.35 + ₹45.60 = ₹288.70. Each scenario value is a sum of parts: FY28E core EBITDA × EV/EBITDA multiple, plus 62.5% of GEML FY28E revenue × EV/Sales, plus Greaves Finance at ₹150 crore, plus ₹38 crore net cash adjustment, minus funding leakage in the bear case only, divided by 23.2951 crore shares. Annualised return = (value ÷ price)^(1/2) − 1.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Bull: ₹547 crore core EBITDA (14.5% margin) at 16x, GEML revenue ₹2,025 crore at 0.8x. Base: ₹488 crore (13.5%) at 13x, GEML ₹1,872 crore at 0.45x. Bear: ₹348 crore (11.0%) at 9.5x, GEML ₹1,495 crore at 0.2x, with ₹150 crore of further GEML funding leaking to Greaves. Cash and investments ₹606 crore, borrowings ₹513 crore and leases ₹55 crore are from the September 2026 balance sheet [2][118].
web_blocks.the_range: ₹152 in the bear case to ₹427 in the bull case. The bear value is above the 52-week low of ₹119.99, so it assumes the business stays intact but earns less [108][118].
web_blocks.if_off: If the base case used the P/E cross-check of about ₹273 instead of ₹303, the weighted value would fall to ₹275.2, about 10.4% a year from ₹225.97 (below a 12% hurdle) and about 15.0% a year from ₹208.14 (our calculation [118]).

web_blocks.caption: Bull, base and bear over 24 months, measured from the live close and from the support level
rows: Bull
Core margin reaches 14.5% on 20% and 18% growth, GEML revenue hits ₹2,025 crore and is valued at 0.8x sales, and the market pays 16x for core EBITDA.
Base
Core margin recovers to 13.5% on 18% and 15% growth, GEML revenue reaches ₹1,872 crore at 0.45x, and core EBITDA is valued at 13x.
Bear
Margin stays near 11% on 10% and 8% growth, GEML needs another ₹150 crore from Greaves, and core EBITDA is valued at 9.5x.
Weighted
web_blocks.takeaway: Per-year figures come from our calculation [118]. From ₹225.97 the weighted return of about 13.0% a year clears a 12% hurdle by one point, which is no cushion given how soft the inputs are. From ₹208.14 it is about 17.8% a year, and that gap is the whole case for waiting.

web_blocks.text: Two inputs are judgment, not market facts: the base multiples of 13x core EBITDA and 0.45x GEML EV/Sales (enterprise value divided by revenue) are our choices [118]. For scale, the whole group trades at 20.1x trailing EV/EBITDA on ₹260 crore of EBITDA, a figure pulled down by GEML’s losses, and peers trade at trailing P/E of 48–56x [118][112][113][114]. A cross-check on earnings is more conservative. Base-case FY28E owner EPS (earnings per share after minority losses) of about ₹9.1 at 30x gives about ₹273, which is about 10% below the ₹303 base [118]. We publish ₹303 as the base and ask you to treat ₹273 as the sober alternative.

web_blocks.caption: Three-horizon judgment, each with a stance
rows: Short term, 0–6 months
Do not buy at ₹225.97.

The stock rose 11.1% in a week, sits 8.57% above its 10-week EMA, and faces supply between ₹230 and ₹272 [108]. Q3 FY27 results (quarter to 31 December 2026) are due after year-end. No date is in our evidence; Q2 came on 29 October, so we infer early-to-mid February 2027 [24]. Pass-through lag may keep core margin near 12% in that print [62].
A pullback into ₹205.02–211.26 opens a purchase; a close below ₹197.60 closes it.
Medium term, 6–24 months
Favourable from support, marginal at the current price.

Core margin back to 13% or more, GEML EBITDA breakeven, and operating cash flow positive without a supplier-credit lift [24][2]. Weighted return is about 18% a year from support and about 13% from ₹225.97 [118].
Two more negative operating cash flow quarters or a new GEML funding round turns the stance to REJECTED.
Long term, 3–5+ years
Not a compounder today; we do not underwrite the FY30 target.

Gensets, auto engines and Excel can compound, with Greaves at about 4% genset share [30][29]. Against that, GEML absorbs capital, group ROCE is 10.1% against 14.6% at KOEL and 17.4% at TVS, and ₹15,000 crore by FY30 needs far more than organic growth [109][112][114][28].
GEML funding itself and group ROCE rising well above 10.1% would justify a compounder review.
web_blocks.takeaway: The stances differ by horizon on purpose. Near term we refuse to chase; over two years we like the odds only from a lower price; over five years the evidence supports a good cyclical engine business, not yet a compounding machine [1][6].

web_blocks.text: Why not IMMEDIATE_BUY? First, business quality is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL, not a compounder pass, because group operating cash flow is negative and debt is rising [2][6]. Second, the stock is extended after an 11% weekly jump [108]. Third, the 13% a year from the live close barely clears the hurdle, and it falls to 10.4% if the conservative P/E cross-check replaces our base [118]. Why not REJECTED? The core is real, with margins of 13–14% for three years and net cash of ₹110 crore [6][62]. The asymmetry from support is 6.7:1, far above the 1.5:1 line below which the rule says reject, and the long-term trend is intact [108]. Anti-hedging in plain words: WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT is a price instruction, not a shrug. We would not buy at ₹225.97, we would buy at a stated zone, and we would be content to miss the stock if it never returns.

Asymmetry means reward to the base value divided by risk to the stop. From the top of the zone it is (₹303 − ₹211.26) ÷ (₹211.26 − ₹197.60) = 6.7:1. At ₹225.97 it is (₹303 − ₹225.97) ÷ (₹225.97 − ₹197.60) = 2.7:1. Both clear the 1.5:1 gate [118], but that gate measures risk only to the stop; the next table measures it against our own bear value. The ratio mixes a 24-month target with a near-term stop, so it measures entry quality and is not a forecast. The stop is also tight: ₹13.66 below the zone top against an ATR (average true range, the typical daily swing) of ₹9.79, about 1.4 ATR, so normal noise could stop us out [108]. Sizing is by risk unit. Under TIER_3 the risk budget is 50 basis points of net worth, which is about ₹21,460 on ₹42.92 lakh. Dividing by the ₹13.66 stop gap gives about 1,570 shares before the tier cap (our calculation [118]). The sizing table that follows is the authoritative version.

rows: Stop ₹197.60 (the verdict rule)

web_blocks.takeaway: The stop-based ratio is the verdict rule and it is high because the stop sits close below the zone. Measured against the ₹152 bear value, the zone offers 1.3:1 to 1.55:1 and the close offers 0.85:1 to 1.04:1. That is why we pay only at the zone and never at the close, and why the pullback, not the stock, carries the verdict [118].

web_blocks.text: A stress test of the verdict makes the same point and we accept it. Shift 15 points of probability toward the bear case (20% bull, 35% base, 45% bear) and the weighted value falls to ₹259.8: +15.0% from the close, about 7.2% a year, and +24.8% from ₹208.14, about 11.7% a year [118]. We stay at WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT rather than REJECTED because the core earns its keep, the stop-based gate clears and the return from the zone stays just under the 12% hurdle (11.7% a year) even after a bearish reweighting, which is why sizing stays at zero today. The wait itself comes from the CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL business label and from the thin one-point margin over the hurdle at the close. It does not come from a breach of any extension limit: the stock is 8.57% above its 10-week average against a 10% cap, and its RSI is 66.5 against a 73 cap [108].

Cash flow deserves a count. Group operating cash flow was negative in FY22, FY23, FY24, FY25 and H1 FY27 and positive only in FY26 at ₹33 crore, so five of the last six reported periods were negative [60][2]. On the 29 October 2026 call the CFO said Greaves does not expect further GEML funding for the next 12 to 18 months, which runs to between October 2027 and April 2028, inside our 24-month horizon [24]. A further round is therefore a live risk on the bear path, where we price it as a ₹150 crore leak, and it is a named downgrade trigger below.

web_blocks.intro: A support zone is the price band where a pullback should meet buyers, and a stop is the price at which we conclude the idea has failed. Greaves sits 8.6% above its 10-week average, so nothing is bought today. The zone is ₹205.02–₹211.26 and the stop is ₹197.60; the table shows how large a first purchase the risk budget allows if the pullback arrives and the KPI alerts are clear.

web_blocks.text: GREAVESCOT is NOT_HELD: the positions ledger of 13 November 2026 shows no Greaves shares, against net worth of ₹42.92 lakh, equities of ₹37.17 lakh and cash of ₹5.75 lakh (13.4% of net worth). With zero shares, no sell instruction applies. The alerts below are advisory conditions to review, not broker orders.

web_blocks.text: Portfolio overlap matters more than the stock’s own story. The Zerodha account already carries SEDEMAC at 14.52%, TDPOWERSYS at 6.85%, TARIL at 6.25%, APARINDS at 6.02% and JYOTICNC at 2.5%, about 36% in total (our sum of the ledger weights). These are auto and industrial cyclicals. A Greaves purchase would add more of the same economic beta, and its one-year beta is not available to us. That argues for the small size the risk-unit rule gives, not for a bigger bet.

web_blocks.text: Upgrade trigger: a daily close above ₹271.90, the 52-week high, on rising volume together with Q3 FY27 core EBITDA margin of 13% or more starts an upgrade review of the verdict.
Reject trigger: a daily close below ₹197.60 cancels any pending buy and sends the stock back for re-underwriting.
Downgrade trigger: two more quarters of negative operating cash flow, or another GEML funding round, moves the verdict to REJECTED.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: If the stock never returns to ₹205.02–211.26 and rises to ₹271.90 without us, will you call the discipline wrong, or will you ask whether the evidence at ₹225.97 ever justified paying for it?
Which of the three KPI alerts would you accept first as proof that the core thesis is intact: margin, cash flow or a GEML funding pause, and why that one?
Where is your own hedge in this chapter: could you state in one sentence what you would do tomorrow, and what price or event would make you stop doing it?

book_paragraphs: Picture a Friday evening in November. You and I have the chart open and the stock has just closed up 1.25% at ₹225.97, after rising 11% in a week. The temptation is obvious. Greaves has a famous old name, a clean-looking uptrend, and a new management team that speaks plainly. Everyone around you seems to be saying the stock has finally turned. This last chapter is where all the evidence meets a price, and a price is where feelings turn into decisions.

Let us begin by arguing the other side of our own conclusion, because a verdict is worth little until it has survived its best enemy. First the bull, and I want you to hear him at full volume. He says the engine business is a real business. For three years the standalone margin sat at 13% to 14%. Gensets of medium size grew 35%, three-wheeler engines 37%, the cable maker 30%. The scooter business, once bleeding about ₹20,000 on every sale, now loses about ₹6,300. A ₹530 crore rights issue, with the Abdul Latif Jameel partner paying nearly ₹199 crore, has bought 12 to 18 months of runway. The people at the top are new, and the CFO says plainly that the group has ₹606 crore of cash against ₹513 crore of borrowings. Why would you stand aside from that?

Now the bear, with equal force. He says look at the cash. In the first half of this year the group's operating cash flow was minus ₹212 crore. Over five years it was negative while the company reported positive operating profit. Core margin fell from 14.9% to 12.0% on 20% more revenue, and the chief executive himself said the improvement had been slower than anticipated. The scooter unit still lost ₹63 crore at the operating line in six months and has no breakeven date, only management's words, fairly soon. The last time the subsidy rules turned, the company lost about ₹477 crore and volume fell 56% in a year. And the stated ambition of ₹15,000 crore by FY30 needs growth that, on the arithmetic of Chapter 5, we rate well under one chance in ten.

So who wins? Neither wins outright, and that is exactly why we turn to probabilities rather than slogans. We gave the bull 25%, the base 45% and the bear 30%. In the bull world the core margin reaches 14.5% and the market pays 16 times core operating profit, giving ₹427 a share. In the base world the margin recovers to 13.5% and the multiple is 13 times, giving ₹303. In the bear world margin stays near 11%, the scooter business asks for another ₹150 crore, and the stock is worth ₹152. Multiply and add and you get ₹288.7, which is 27.8% above the live price over two years, about 13% a year.

The scooter business deserves one more look, because it is where the bull and the bear are both most certain. The market has shown you both endings in a single year. One listed electric two-wheeler maker has seen revenue fall about 49% over the last twelve months with an operating margin near minus 94%. Another, much larger in market value, is valued for its scale even though it still loses money at the operating line. Greaves Electric sits somewhere between them, with revenue doubling and a smaller loss per vehicle. Our weighting does not say it will succeed. It says that the base case values each rupee of its sales at about 45 paise, and the bear case values it at 20 paise and charges the parent another ₹150 crore.

Now I want to be honest about the soft spots in that number, because a precise-looking figure can fool you. The base uses 13 times core earnings before interest, tax and depreciation, and 0.45 times sales for the scooter company. Those are our judgments, not market prints. A second check, which values the group on earnings after minority losses at 30 times, gives about ₹273 rather than ₹303. If we used it for the base case, the weighted value would fall to about ₹275, and the annual return from today's price would drop to about 10%, below a 12% hurdle. So at ₹225.97 you are being paid roughly the hurdle if the model is right and less if it is slightly wrong.

Compare that with buying lower. From ₹208.14, the level where the ten-week moving average sits, the same weighted value gives about 17.8% a year. The base case alone gives about 20.7%. The upside barely changes; the price you pay does. That is Benjamin Graham's margin of safety in one picture. You do not need a better forecast. You need a cheaper entry. Our zone is ₹205.02 to ₹211.26, and if the stock closes below ₹197.60 we walk away rather than argue with it.

I should also tell you what the numbers do not say. The ratio of reward to risk from the top of the zone is 6.7 to 1, and at today's price it is 2.7 to 1. Both clear the 1.5 line, which is the rule below which we would reject the stock. But that ratio compares a two-year target with a near-term stop, so it tells you about the quality of an entry, not about what will happen. The stop is also tight. Thirteen rupees sixty-six sit between the top of the zone and the stop, and the stock's typical daily swing is nearly ten rupees. You could be stopped out by noise and then watch the stock recover. A stop protects the plan; it does not promise a result.

Why not buy now, then? Three reasons, and you can test each yourself. The business is conditional, not a compounder: it is good at the core and unproven at the group level, because cash flow is negative and debt has risen. The price is stretched after a one-week jump. And the return from here only just clears the hurdle. Why not reject the stock? Because the core is genuine, the trend is intact, and from support the odds are lopsided in your favour. When a verdict sits between those two answers, the honest word is wait, and we say it with numbers attached.

Think about time as three separate clocks. In the next six months you should not chase. Third-quarter results are likely in early to mid February 2027, though the company has not told us the date in anything we read, and metal costs may still be squeezing the core. Over the next two years we like the stock from a lower price, because margin back to 13% or more, a scooter breakeven and positive operating cash flow are all plausible. Over five years we do not yet call it a compounder. Gensets, engines and cables can compound, but the scooter unit consumes capital and the group still earns about 10% on what it employs.

There is also the question of what you already own. In the Zerodha account Greaves is not held, so there is nothing to sell and no tax lot to worry about. But the book is full of cousins. SEDEMAC is 14.52% of the portfolio, TDPOWERSYS 6.85%, TARIL 6.25%, APARINDS 6.02% and JYOTICNC 2.5%. Together that is about 36% in auto and industrial cyclicals that tend to fall on the same bad days. A Greaves purchase would add to that bunch, so it earns a small, risk-sized position, not a big one. The risk budget is 50 basis points of your net worth of ₹42.92 lakh, which is about ₹21,460 of loss at the stop.

What does the money do in the meantime? We checked every place the next rupee could go. Cash stays at 100%, because nothing clears price, quality and reward-to-risk together today. AJMERA, on the shortlist, is cheaper on earnings at about 15.5 times and has a reward-to-risk of 5.2, but at ₹133.28 it sits just above its own zone of ₹124.51 to ₹132.17. Greaves is a zero today and becomes fundable only on a pullback into its zone. Charlie Munger said the big money is not in the buying and selling but in the waiting. The waiting is only worth something if the conditions are written down first.

A word on what we are not claiming. The live price of ₹225.97 is the 13 November close from a snapshot taken after the market shut, while the ledger still carries the 12 November bar at ₹223.18. A weekly market dashboard dated 8 November does not list Greaves among its rising-trend names, so the chart is our only confirmation of strength, and the stock is not tradable in options. Each of these is a reason to size small and keep the stop honest. None of them is a reason to ignore the trend, which is genuinely above every key average.

Finally, here is what would change our mind. If the stock closes above ₹271.90, the 52-week high, on strong volume and the third-quarter core margin is 13% or better, we reopen the case for an upgrade. If it closes below ₹197.60, we reject or re-underwrite. And if two more quarters pass with negative operating cash flow, or the scooter company asks for another round of money, the verdict becomes rejected. Notice that each trigger is a price or a fact you can look up, not a mood. That is the test of an honest verdict: could someone else check, next quarter, whether you were right?

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Charlie Munger said the big money is not in the buying and selling but in the waiting. Waiting is easy when you know what you are waiting for and hard when you do not. Write down the price, the stop and the three facts that would end the wait. Then see whether the day's news moves you, or only the list.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Benjamin Graham gave us three words, margin of safety. Ask what yours is here. Is it the cheaper entry at ₹208.14, the net cash at the core, or the stop? A good answer names a number. A weak one names a hope.

web_title: 9. Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan
question: Bull or bear, what should you do with new money, and where should it wait?
